children.value: A valid Stratum specification must satisfy seven semantic invariants. These invariants ensure that every specification is not only syntactically well-formed but also semantically coherent, traceable, and verifiable. Together, they form the foundation for trustworthy system documentation that can be automatically validated and maintained over time.

Each invariant addresses a distinct aspect of specification quality: G1 (Provenance) ensures traceability to purpose; G2 (Fulfillment) ensures completeness; G3 (Non-Contradiction) ensures consistency; G4 (Materialization) ensures groundedness; G5 (Predictability) enables impact analysis; G6 (Stratification) enforces abstraction boundaries; and G7 (Diagnosability) provides actionable error reporting.

These seven invariants have deep roots in 40+ years of academic literature, industry standards, and formal methods. Each property maps to established concepts from IEEE/ISO standards, SEI publications, OMG specifications, and foundational computer science research.

The Provenance guarantee (G1) corresponds to **bidirectional traceability** in requirements engineering literature. IEEE 24765 defines traceability as "the degree to which each element in a software development product establishes its reason for existing." ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148:2018 requires that traceable requirements be "upwards traceable to specific documented stakeholder statement(s) of need... and downwards traceable to the specific requirements in the lower tier requirements specification."

The Provenance guarantee ensures that every element in a specification can trace its existence back to a root purpose. Nothing exists without justification—every requirement, design decision, and implementation detail must be connected to the fundamental goals of the system. This prevents orphaned elements that serve no purpose and ensures complete traceability from implementation to intent.

Safety-critical standards enforce this rigorously. DO-178C requires that "every line of code must be traceable to a requirement" (Table A-7, Objective 9). IEC 61508-3 Annex A.1 specifies that backward traceability checks "that the implementation is justified by a requirement"—the core provenance property. In formal methods, the refinement calculus (Back & von Wright 1998) provides mathematical foundations where each refinement step is proven to preserve specification truth.

attributes.statement: root(e) ≡ layer(e).stratum = purpose ∧ ¬∃d ∈ D. d.tgt.elem = e.id ∧ d.δ = justified_by
tracePath(e) = shortest path from e to some e' where root(e') following justified_by dependencies from target to source (impl → requirement)
attributes.note: Analogous to Gotel & Finkelstein's forward/backward traceability links

children.value: ∀ e ∈ E. ∃ e' ∈ E. root(e') ∧ reachable(e, e', justified_by)
Every element in the specification must be reachable from a root element in the purpose stratum via justified_by dependencies, which flow from implementation toward requirement.

Formally, for specification S:
Provenanced(S) ≡ ∀ e ∈ elements(S). tracePath(e) ≠ ∅

The Fulfillment guarantee (G2) corresponds to **constraint satisfaction** and **model satisfaction** (M ⊨ S) in formal logic. Contract-based design (Benveniste et al. 2018) formalizes this through assume-guarantee contracts where a component satisfies a contract if "all runs that satisfy assumptions A must satisfy guarantees G." The compositional theorem states that if all components satisfy their own contracts, a global system contract is satisfied.

The Fulfillment guarantee ensures that a specification satisfies its own declared constraints. Every specification may declare constraints—rules that must hold for the specification to be considered complete. Fulfillment requires that all error-level constraints evaluate to true. This makes the specification self-validating: it defines its own completeness criteria and then meets them.

IEEE 29148:2018 defines "complete" for individual requirements as "needs no further amplification because it is measurable and sufficiently describes the capability." DO-178C specifies 71 verification objectives organized by Design Assurance Level, with completeness requiring evidence that "each phase is complete, coherent, and traceable to its predecessor." The OMG OCL 2.4 Specification requires that "an OCL expression is an invariant of the type and must be true for all instances of that type at any time."

attributes.note: Model satisfaction relation from formal logic

children.value: ∀ c ∈ ErrorConstraints(S). S ⊨ c
Every error-level constraint declared in the specification must evaluate to true. This ensures completeness relative to the specification's own stated requirements.

Complexity: evaluating all error constraints is O(|C_error| * T_eval), where T_eval is the cost of a single constraint evaluation over E and D. For finite, quantifier-bounded constraints, this is typically polynomial in |E| + |D|.

Formally:
Fulfilled(S) ≡ ∀ c ∈ ErrorConstraints(S). c.φ(E, D) = ⊤
Common fulfillment constraints:
∀ feature f. ∃ test t. tests(t, f) - Feature test coverage
∀ api a. ∃ doc d. documents(d, a) - API documentation
∀ aggregate ag. ∃ command c. commands(ag, c) - Aggregate has commands

The Non-Contradiction guarantee (G3) maps to **internal consistency** and **satisfiability** in formal methods. The classical Law of Non-Contradiction (Aristotle) states ¬(P ∧ ¬P). In SAT/SMT solving, this becomes satisfiability: a set of constraints is consistent iff their conjunction is satisfiable. VDM explicitly defines proof obligations for internal consistency: "A proof obligation is a theorem stating that a certain property must hold in order for a formal specification to be internally consistent."

The Non-Contradiction guarantee prevents semantic conflicts within a specification. When two elements make claims about the same property—such as an API's return type appearing in both the interface definition and its handler implementation—those claims must agree. Contradiction detection identifies cases where elements that should unify actually assert incompatible values, catching integration errors before they manifest as runtime bugs.

For TLA+ specifications, Lamport defines invariants as "state predicates true of all reachable states," with the TLC model checker performing breadth-first search to verify invariance. In Alloy, consistency analysis uses SAT-based model finding: a specification is consistent if at least one valid instance exists that satisfies all facts within a bounded scope. IEEE 29148:2018 requires that requirements be "consistent: free of conflicts with other requirements." The KAOS methodology formally defines conflicts as goals that are "mutually inconsistent under domain axioms."

attributes.statement: contradiction(e₁, e₂) ≡ ∃ property p. e₁.π(p) is defined ∧ e₂.π(p) is defined ∧ e₁.π(p) ≠ e₂.π(p) ∧ unifies(e₁, e₂, p)
attributes.note: Two elements contradict when they both define a property p, assert different values, and a unification constraint requires them to match. Maps to SAT/SMT conflict detection.

attributes.statement: unifies(e₁, e₂, p) ≡ ∃ c ∈ C. c.cat = non_contradiction ∧ c specifies e₁.p must equal e₂.p

children.value: ∀ e₁, e₂ ∈ E. ¬contradiction(e₁, e₂)
No pair of elements may assert incompatible values for any property that a unification constraint requires to match. This prevents semantic conflicts within the specification.

Complexity: a direct check over all constrained pairs is O(|E|^2 * k), where k is the average number of properties compared. With indexed constraints and candidate pairing, this can be reduced to O(|D| + |E| * k) in typical implementations.

Formally:
NonContradictory(S) ≡ ∀ e₁, e₂ ∈ elements(S). ¬contradiction(e₁, e₂)
Common non-contradiction constraints:
API return type = Handler return type
Event schema = Event handler expected schema
Database field type = Domain entity field type

The Materialization guarantee (G4) builds on **refinement** and **reification** theory with a 40-year history. C.B. Jones's VDM work defines reification as "finding a more concrete representation of abstract data types"—stepwise transformation with proof obligations via retrieve functions. The He-Hoare-Sanders formulation (1986) introduces downward and upward simulation with abstraction relations ρ ⊆ Σ_A × Σ_C between abstract and concrete states.

The Materialization guarantee ensures that abstract specifications are grounded in concrete reality. Every element at the physical stratum—the lowest level of abstraction—must have a binding that connects it to an actual artifact: a file, a database table, a hardware component. This prevents specifications from describing phantom systems that exist only on paper, ensuring that what is specified actually exists.

Enterprise architecture uses the **realization relationship** (ArchiMate 3.2): "A dependency relationship that connects a logical entity with a more concrete entity that implements it." The progression flows from Architecture Building Blocks (ABBs) to Solution Building Blocks (SBBs). In MDA, the transformation chain CIM → PIM → PSM → Code represents progressive materialization. A specification is "fully grounded" when the Platform Specific Model produces deployable Executable Object Code.

attributes.note: Analogous to VDM reification retrieve functions

children.value: ∀ e ∈ E. terminal(e) → materialized(e)
Every element at the physical stratum must have an associated binding that maps it to a concrete artifact. This ensures specifications describe things that actually exist.

Formally:
Materialized(S) ≡ ∀ e ∈ elements(S). terminal(e) → materialized(e)
Complexity: checking bindings for terminal elements is O(|E_terminal| × |B|) with naive lookup, or O(|E_terminal|) with indexed bindings where each terminal element has O(1) binding lookup.
Materialization types per domain:
Software: Component → File:Line
Manufacturing: Part → Drawing + BOM
Healthcare: Protocol → EMR Configuration
Legal: Clause → Document Section

The Predictability guarantee (G5) connects to **modifiability** and **change impact analysis** research. The SEI defines modifiability as "a quality attribute that relates to the cost of change and refers to the ease with which a software system can accommodate changes." Bohner & Arnold's foundational 1996 work defines change impact analysis as "identifying the potential consequences of a change, or estimating what needs to be modified to accomplish a change."

The Predictability guarantee enables reliable change impact analysis. Before any change is applied to a specification, the complete set of affected elements can be computed in linear time. This allows teams to understand the full consequences of a proposed change—which tests need to run, which documents need updating, which stakeholders need notification—before committing to it.

Reps, Horwitz, and Sagiv's POPL 1995 paper on IFDS problems provides "a polynomial-time algorithm for finding precise solutions to a general class of interprocedural dataflow-analysis problems." The incremental model transformation literature (VIATRA framework) establishes that "synchronization time is proportional to the magnitude of change and not to the size of models"—precisely the property Predictable(S) requires. Yau & Collofello's ripple effect analysis (IEEE TSE 1985) measures structural stability upon modification.

attributes.statement: δ ::= ⟨element: ID, changeType: CHANGE, details: VALUE⟩
impact(S, δ) = ⋃ {cascade(S, elem(δ), δ.changeType, r) | r ∈ R, r.trigger matches δ}
attributes.note: Analogous to Bohner & Arnold's ripple effect propagation

children.value: ∀ δ : CHANGE. impact(S, δ) is computable before applying δ

For any proposed change δ, the complete set of affected elements and their effects can be computed in O(|E| + |D|) time before the change is applied. This enables reliable impact analysis and risk assessment.

Formally:
Predictable(S) ≡ impact : S × CHANGE → P(E × EFFECT) is total and computable in O(|E| + |D|) time
This enables:
Pre-change impact analysis
Automated change review
Risk assessment
Staged rollout decisions

The Stratification guarantee (G6) embodies **layered abstraction** and Robert C. Martin's **Dependency Rule**: "Source code dependencies can only point inwards. Nothing in an inner circle can know anything at all about something in an outer circle." A crucial distinction from Abelson & Sussman's work (1987): "Where layers are levels of equal abstraction in software, strata are levels of different abstraction." Layers provide horizontal separation by functional concern; strata provide vertical separation by abstraction level.

The Stratification guarantee enforces clean abstraction boundaries. Dependencies must flow downward through the strata (from purpose through logical to physical), preventing implementation details from leaking into high-level requirements. The sole exception is the justified_by relation, which explicitly links implementations back to the requirements they satisfy—flowing upward to establish provenance.

ArchiMate's three core layers (Business, Application, Technology) formalize this with "higher layers making use of services provided by lower layers" and realization relationships connecting elements across layers. OMG's MOF four-layer metamodel architecture (M0-M3) provides rigorous formalization: "Models at every level conform to a model belonging to the upper level." MOF is closed—M3 conforms to itself. MDA's CIM/PIM/PSM separation achieves vertical separation of concerns with transformations flowing downward.

attributes.statement: stratumRespecting(d) ≡ let l_s = layer(src(d)), l_t = layer(tgt(d)) in
attributes.note: Analogous to Martin's Dependency Rule

children.value: rank(l_s) ≥ rank(l_t) ∨ d.δ = justified_by

attributes.label: STRATIFICATION
attributes.standardRefs: Martin Clean Architecture 2017, OMG MDA, MOF M0-M3

children.value: ∀ d ∈ D. stratumRespecting(d)

Dependencies must respect stratum boundaries: elements may only depend on elements at equal or lower rank. The justified_by relation is the sole exception, explicitly linking implementations to their requirements.

Formally:
Stratified(S) ≡ ∀ d ∈ dependencies(S). stratumRespecting(d)

Complexity: a single pass over all dependencies, O(|D|). Each dependency check requires O(1) stratum rank lookup for source and target elements, making the total verification linear in the number of dependencies.
This ensures:
Abstraction boundaries are respected
Implementation details don't leak upward
Changes cascade predictably (down, not up)
Exception: justified_by dependencies go UP (from impl to requirement)

The Diagnosability guarantee (G7) leverages **MUS extraction** and **model-based diagnosis** from SAT/SMT theory. A Minimal Unsatisfiable Subset (MUS) is a subset M of an unsatisfiable formula F where M is unsatisfiable but removing any clause makes it satisfiable. Reiter's seminal 1987 paper establishes that "the set of diagnoses is exactly the set of minimal hitting sets of the collection of all conflicts." Junker's QuickXplain algorithm (2004) efficiently computes preferred minimal conflicts using divide-and-conquer with O(n·log(k+1)+k²) consistency checks.

When validation fails, humans need actionable explanations. G7 requires that every violation report includes an irreducible unsat core—the minimal set of constraints causing the failure—and human-readable diagnostic text.

Diagnosability from discrete-event systems theory (Sampath et al. 1995) defines when faults can be unambiguously detected: fault f is diagnosable iff no two infinite runs exist with identical observable projections where f occurs in one but not the other. The hitting set duality—every MUS hits every MCS (Minimal Correction Subset)—enables computing repairs from conflicts. Delta debugging (Zeller 1999) provides 1-minimality for failure-inducing inputs.

attributes.note: Structure based on Reiter's theory of diagnosis from first principles

Every validation failure must produce a diagnosis containing an irreducible minimal conflict set. This enables precise identification of the root cause and supports automated remediation.

Formally:

**Implementation**: Use SMT solver unsat core extraction (Z3 `unsat_core()`, CVC5 `getUnsatCore()`). See Theorem 10.12 for irreducibility proof obligation.
**Conformance**: G7 is **K1 (Certified-Aware)**, not K0. K0 implementations may return violations without explanations. K1+ implementations MUST provide irreducible unsat cores per Theorem 10.12.

The seven invariants combine to form the definition of a valid specification. A specification that satisfies all invariants is one that can be trusted: it is traceable to purpose, internally consistent, grounded in reality, and when it fails validation, it explains why. This is the central quality criterion for any Stratum document.

attributes.statement: Valid(S) ≡ WellFormed(S) ∧ Provenanced(S) ∧ Fulfilled(S) ∧ NonContradictory(S) ∧ Materialized(S) ∧ Predictable(S) ∧ Stratified(S) ∧ Diagnosable(S)

children.value: A specification is valid iff it is well-formed and satisfies all seven invariants. Note: G7 (Diagnosability) is K1 conformance; K0 implementations check G1-G6 only.
The following table summarizes how each Stratum guarantee maps to established terminology in formal methods, requirements engineering, and safety-critical standards:

| Stratum Property | Primary Established Term | Key Standards/Papers |
|------------------|-------------------------|---------------------|
| G1: Provenanced(S) | Bidirectional traceability | IEEE 29148:2018, DO-178C, Gotel & Finkelstein 1994 |
| G2: Fulfilled(S) | Constraint satisfaction | IEEE 29148:2018, Benveniste et al. 2018 |
| G3: NonContradictory(S) | Internal consistency | VDM Proof Obligations, Lamport TLA+ 2002 |
| G4: Materialized(S) | Reification/Refinement | Jones VDM 1990, ArchiMate 3.2, DO-178C |
| G5: Predictable(S) | Modifiability | SEI CMU/SEI-2007-TR-002, Bohner & Arnold 1996 |
| G6: Stratified(S) | Layered abstraction | Martin Clean Architecture 2017, OMG MDA, MOF M0-M3 |
| G7: Diagnosable(S) | Minimal unsatisfiable subset | Reiter 1987, Junker QuickXplain 2004, Sampath 1995 |

IEEE/ISO standards, OMG specifications (MOF, OCL, MDA), and safety-critical standards (DO-178C, ISO 26262, IEC 61508) independently arrived at nearly identical property definitions, suggesting these validity properties are fundamental to rigorous specification. Every Stratum property maps to concepts with 30-40 years of formal methods research.
The following references provide the foundational research grounding for Stratum's semantic invariants. References are organized by the guarantee they primarily support.

attributes.title: An Analysis of the Requirements Traceability Problem
attributes.author: Gotel, Orlena C. Z. and Finkelstein, Anthony C. W.
attributes.booktitle: Proceedings of the First IEEE International Conference on Requirements Engineering (ICRE'94)
attributes.note: Foundational paper defining requirements traceability. Introduces the distinction between pre-requirements specification (pre-RS) and post-requirements specification (post-RS) traceability.

attributes.title: ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148:2018 Systems and software engineering — Life cycle processes — Requirements engineering
attributes.author: ISO/IEC/IEEE
attributes.note: International standard defining requirements engineering processes. Section 5.2.8 specifies bidirectional traceability requirements. Section 6.2 defines nine characteristics for well-formed requirements: necessary, appropriate, unambiguous, complete, singular, feasible, verifiable, correct, and conforming.

attributes.title: DO-178C: Software Considerations in Airborne Systems and Equipment Certification
attributes.author: RTCA, Inc.
attributes.note: Primary safety standard for airborne software. Table A-7 specifies traceability objectives including Objective 9: verification of additional code that cannot be traced to Source Code. Defines 71 verification objectives organized by Design Assurance Level (DAL). Requires 100% requirements coverage and no orphan code.

attributes.title: Refinement Calculus: A Systematic Introduction
attributes.author: Back, Ralph-Johan and von Wright, Joakim
attributes.note: Comprehensive treatment of refinement calculus. Provides mathematical foundations where each refinement step is proven to preserve specification truth. Introduces the refinement relation ⊑ and proves compositionality theorems.

attributes.title: Toward Reference Models for Requirements Traceability
attributes.author: Ramesh, Balasubramaniam and Jarke, Matthias
attributes.note: Presents a comprehensive reference model for requirements traceability based on empirical study of 26 organizations. Distinguishes between low-end and high-end traceability practices.

attributes.title: Contracts for System Design
attributes.author: Benveniste, Albert and Caillaud, Benoît and Nickovic, Dejan and Passerone, Roberto and Raclet, Jean-Baptiste and Reinkemeier, Philipp and Sangiovanni-Vincentelli, Alberto and Damm, Werner and Henzinger, Thomas A. and Larsen, Kim G.
attributes.journal: Foundations and Trends in Electronic Design Automation
attributes.note: Comprehensive survey of contract-based design. Formalizes assume-guarantee contracts: a component satisfies contract (A,G) if all runs satisfying assumptions A also satisfy guarantees G. Proves compositional theorem: if all components satisfy their contracts, the composed system satisfies the global contract.

attributes.title: Object Constraint Language (OCL) Version 2.4
attributes.author: Object Management Group
attributes.note: OMG formal specification formal/2014-02-03. States: 'OCL is a typed language so that each OCL expression has a type. To be well formed, an OCL expression must conform to the type conformance rules of the language.' Sections 8.3.7, 10.2.2, 11.3-11.7 define well-formedness rules. Requires invariants to be true for all instances at all times.

attributes.title: Systematic Software Development using VDM
attributes.author: Jones, Cliff B.
attributes.note: Definitive VDM reference. Defines reification as 'finding a more concrete representation of abstract data types' with proof obligations via retrieve functions. Chapter 8 covers data reification; Chapter 9 covers operation decomposition. Introduces proof obligations for internal consistency.

attributes.title: Specifying Systems: The TLA+ Language and Tools for Hardware and Software Engineers
attributes.author: Lamport, Leslie
attributes.note: Comprehensive TLA+ guide. Defines invariants as 'state predicates true of all reachable states.' The TLC model checker performs breadth-first search to verify invariance. Chapter 14 covers the model checker; Chapter 5 covers invariants and safety properties.

attributes.title: Software Abstractions: Logic, Language, and Analysis
attributes.author: Jackson, Daniel
attributes.note: Alloy language and analyzer reference. Explains SAT-based consistency analysis: a specification is consistent if at least one valid instance exists satisfying all facts within a bounded scope. Introduces 'small scope hypothesis' for bounded verification.

attributes.title: Requirements Engineering: From System Goals to UML Models to Software Specifications
attributes.author: van Lamsweerde, Axel
attributes.note: Comprehensive RE text covering KAOS methodology. Formally defines conflicts as goals that are 'mutually inconsistent under domain axioms' and divergences as weaker conflicts occurring under boundary conditions. Chapter 8 covers conflict management.

attributes.title: Data Refinement Refined
attributes.author: He, Jifeng and Hoare, C. A. R. and Sanders, Jeff W.
attributes.note: Introduces downward and upward simulation with abstraction relations ρ ⊆ Σ_A × Σ_C between abstract and concrete states. Proves joint completeness: using both simulation notions ensures sound refinement.

attributes.title: ArchiMate 3.2 Specification
attributes.author: The Open Group
attributes.note: Enterprise architecture modeling standard. Defines realization relationship as 'a dependency relationship that connects a logical entity with a more concrete entity that implements it.' Specifies three core layers: Business, Application, Technology with 'higher layers making use of services provided by lower layers.'

attributes.title: MDA Guide Version 2.0
attributes.author: Object Management Group
attributes.note: OMG Model Driven Architecture guide. Defines CIM/PIM/PSM transformation chain representing progressive materialization. A specification is 'fully grounded' when PSM produces deployable Executable Object Code.

attributes.title: Modifiability Tactics
attributes.author: Bachmann, Felix and Bass, Len and Nord, Robert
attributes.institution: Software Engineering Institute, Carnegie Mellon University
attributes.note: SEI technical report on modifiability. Defines modifiability as 'a quality attribute that relates to the cost of change and refers to the ease with which a software system can accommodate changes.' Provides cost model: Average cost = direct modification cost + propagated modification costs.

attributes.title: Software Change Impact Analysis
attributes.author: Bohner, Shawn A. and Arnold, Robert S.
attributes.note: Foundational work on change impact analysis. Defines IA as 'identifying the potential consequences of a change, or estimating what needs to be modified to accomplish a change.' Distinguishes traceability-based IA (relationships analyzed for scope) from dependency-based IA (linkages assessed for consequences).

attributes.title: Precise Interprocedural Dataflow Analysis via Graph Reachability
attributes.author: Reps, Thomas and Horwitz, Susan and Sagiv, Mooly
attributes.booktitle: Proceedings of the 22nd ACM SIGPLAN-SIGACT Symposium on Principles of Programming Languages (POPL '95)
attributes.note: Provides polynomial-time algorithm for IFDS problems. When dataflow functions distribute over meet and domain is finite, Tabulation Algorithm runs in O(N·D²). Foundation for precise impact analysis.

attributes.title: Design Stability Measures for Software Maintenance
attributes.author: Yau, Stephen S. and Collofello, James S.
attributes.note: Introduces ripple effect analysis measuring structural stability upon modification using applied probabilities and matrix algebra. Foundation for quantitative impact prediction.

attributes.title: Clean Architecture: A Craftsman's Guide to Software Structure and Design
attributes.author: Martin, Robert C.
attributes.note: Articulates The Dependency Rule: 'Source code dependencies can only point inwards. Nothing in an inner circle can know anything at all about something in an outer circle.' Layers (inner to outer): Entities, Use Cases, Interface Adapters, Frameworks & Drivers. 'As you move inwards, the level of abstraction increases.'

attributes.title: Lisp: A Language for Stratified Design
attributes.author: Abelson, Harold and Sussman, Gerald Jay
attributes.note: Distinguishes layers from strata: 'Where layers are levels of equal abstraction in software, strata are levels of different abstraction.' Layers provide horizontal separation by functional concern; strata provide vertical separation by abstraction level.

attributes.title: OMG Meta Object Facility (MOF) Core Specification Version 2.5.1
attributes.author: Object Management Group
attributes.note: ISO/IEC 19508:2014. Provides four-layer metamodel architecture (M0-M3): 'Models at every level conform to a model belonging to the upper level.' MOF is closed—M3 conforms to itself. Uses constraints to define well-formedness rules for metadata.

attributes.title: A Framework for Information Systems Architecture
attributes.author: Zachman, John A.
attributes.note: Foundational enterprise architecture framework. Notes: 'The Rows define TRANSFORMATION, NOT decomposition'—reification through perspectives from contextual through instantiation.

attributes.title: A Theory of Diagnosis from First Principles
attributes.author: Reiter, Raymond
attributes.note: Seminal paper on model-based diagnosis. Establishes: 'the set of diagnoses is exactly the set of minimal hitting sets of the collection of all conflicts.' A conflict set is a set of components whose assumed correct functioning is inconsistent with observations. Hitting set duality enables computing repairs from conflicts.

attributes.title: QUICKXPLAIN: Preferred Explanations and Relaxations for Over-Constrained Problems
attributes.author: Junker, Ulrich
attributes.booktitle: Proceedings of the 19th National Conference on Artificial Intelligence (AAAI-04)
attributes.note: Efficient algorithm for computing preferred minimal conflicts using divide-and-conquer. Complexity: O(n·log(k+1)+k²) consistency checks where n = constraints, k = conflict size. Non-intrusive: works with any propagation mechanism.

attributes.title: Algorithms for Computing Minimal Unsatisfiable Subsets of Constraints
attributes.author: Liffiton, Mark H. and Sakallah, Karem A.
attributes.journal: Journal on Satisfiability, Boolean Modeling and Computation (JSAT)
attributes.note: Comprehensive treatment of MUS extraction algorithms. Defines MUS as subset M of unsatisfiable formula F where M is unsatisfiable but removing any clause makes it satisfiable. Surveys exact and approximation algorithms.

attributes.title: Diagnosability of Discrete-event Systems
attributes.author: Sampath, Meera and Sengupta, Raja and Lafortune, Stéphane and Sinnamohideen, Kasim and Teneketzis, Demosthenis
attributes.note: Defines diagnosability in discrete-event systems: fault f is diagnosable iff no two infinite runs exist with identical observable projections where f occurs in one but not the other. Foundation for fault detection theory.

attributes.title: Diagnosing Multiple Faults
attributes.author: de Kleer, Johan and Williams, Brian C.
attributes.note: Companion paper to Reiter 1987. Develops GDE (General Diagnostic Engine) for diagnosing multiple simultaneous faults. Introduces probabilistic ranking of diagnoses.

attributes.title: Simplifying and Isolating Failure-Inducing Input
attributes.author: Zeller, Andreas and Hildebrandt, Ralf
attributes.note: Introduces delta debugging for 1-minimality: finding minimal failure-inducing configuration where removing any single element produces passing test. Generalizes binary search to arbitrary domains.

attributes.title: On Computing Minimal Correction Subsets
attributes.author: Marques-Silva, Joao and Heras, Federico and Janota, Mikoláš and Previti, Alessandro and Belov, Anton
attributes.booktitle: Proceedings of the 23rd International Joint Conference on Artificial Intelligence (IJCAI-13)
attributes.note: Relates MCS (Minimal Correction Subsets) to MUS via hitting set duality. MCS represents minimal sets of constraints whose removal makes formula satisfiable. Every MUS hits every MCS and vice versa.

attributes.title: A Syntactic Approach to Type Soundness
attributes.author: Wright, Andrew K. and Felleisen, Matthias
attributes.note: Canonical formulation of type soundness via Progress and Preservation theorems: well-typed programs do not 'go wrong' during execution. Foundation for WellFormed(S) decidability.

attributes.title: Types and Programming Languages
attributes.author: Pierce, Benjamin C.
attributes.note: Comprehensive textbook on type theory. Chapter 8 covers type soundness; Chapters 21-32 cover advanced type systems. Standard reference for understanding WellFormed as type-theoretic property.

attributes.title: IEC 61508: Functional Safety of Electrical/Electronic/Programmable Electronic Safety-related Systems
attributes.author: International Electrotechnical Commission
attributes.note: International safety standard. Annex A.1 specifies that backward traceability checks 'that the implementation is justified by a requirement'—the core provenance property. Complements DO-178C for industrial applications.

children.value: **Note on decidability stratification**: Properties WellFormed and NonContradictory have decidable checking procedures (type systems, SAT solvers), while Fulfilled and Provenanced may require semi-decidable or process-based verification depending on the expressiveness of constraint languages used.

**Note on IEEE/OMG/safety-critical convergence**: The independent convergence of IEEE 29148, OMG specifications (MOF, OCL, MDA), and safety-critical standards (DO-178C, ISO 26262, IEC 61508) on nearly identical property definitions suggests these validity properties are fundamental rather than arbitrary design choices.

**Note on formal methods maturity**: Every Stratum property maps to concepts with 30-40 years of formal methods research. This maturity provides confidence in both theoretical soundness and practical implementability via established tools (Z3, CVC5, TLC, Alloy Analyzer, etc.).
